title: I build a No Man’s Sky like game with GPT 6 Astra
author: AIVibeCodeArtist
selftext:
I wanted to test GPT 6 Astra. I’m a fan of No Man’s Sky so I thought to create a similar game experience. 

It is no where near what No Man’s Sky is in terms of detail, gameplay elements, etc. BUT the endless star and galaxy exploration experience is pretty close.

What do you think? 

Play it on https://aster.emmerzaal.com

View demo on: https://youtu.be/UlPSsbo4C\_Y?is=WjzawNc40oKySJhi

replies.author: sirpalee
replies.body:
Yeah, taste, gut feeling, architectural rigor and domain specific knowledge. Also learning and adopting quickly.

The difference between AI and humans is that a good developer designer sees the implicit design elements, how everything is minimal, how everything tries to keep things simple and won't introduce new elements all the time. With AI you need to keep hammering into them, by either having good guidelines or runnig  automated review loops/graphs/harnesses that makes sure things are kept simple and not overdesigned.

comments.author: Cool-Chemical-5629
comments.body: Many people say AI is not able to build whole games in one prompt. This is true for now, but at the same time... When GPT 4 came out, it was barely able to create a simple game of blackjack. The code it produced was so good it impressed me enough to keep it at that time. I had to make some manual fixes to the code (not AI assisted, I fixed the code myself). But look where we are here today. We are creating impressive 3D games using AI. Now consider this. Is it really "one prompt", if you give the task to an AI agent instead of a regular AI chat? It's still a single prompt, but the difference is - the AI can see what it did in last turn and it can go back and fix it if it's told to do so in the prompt. That's something which helps to improve those "one shot" games a lot. I believe we are not that far from "Build me XY game" and the AI agents will do it all by themselves, even download the right tools for the job, all automatically. The progress feels unstoppable now.

replies.author: AvengerDr
replies.body:
If only every technology could follow this progress rate. Just a hundred years ago we had internal combustion engines. Now one hundred years later (and more) we don't have cars that go 1.000 km/h or thst consume next to nothing. They are more efficient but not radically so.

This is to say that LLMs might arrive to a plateau with diminishing returns. It's not granted that they will lead to AGI or anything remotely like it.

replies.author: imnotabot303
replies.body:
What you say is true but people in AI spaces are also very naive to what the outcomes of AI will be if it follows current trajectories and doesn't plateau out in a few years.

Once we reach a point where anyone can just ask for X game and you don't need any game dev  experience at all. Then all indie games become worthless both in monetary terms and to everyone else as a piece of media. Everything basically becomes disposable content. 

Nobody will be interested in seeing your game or anyone else's and definitely won't be interested in paying for it. At that point everyone will just be subscribed to AI services that will produce whatever you ask for on demand. At that point the only people making money from the industry will be the companies providing the AI services and the large game companies that are producing games beyond the scope of indie devs using AI.

This will happen to all creative industries too not just game dev.
